courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Alpha compositing sorted splats at one pixel
md: Pixel color is a weighted sum of splat colors with weights $\alpha_i T_i$. Order changes who gets the weight, and every splat with nonzero weight receives a gradient.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
md: Choose by failure mode. Tagged pointers: cheap, but need wide CAS or spare bits and type-stable nodes. LL/SC: ABA-free in principle, rarely usable directly. Hazard pointers: bounded garbage under stalls, cost per access. Epochs: cheapest per access, but one stalled thread blocks all reclamation.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Who are you, and what may you do: authentication vs authorization
md: Being logged in is not a permission. Authentication tells the server *who* is asking; it says nothing about *which* objects and functions that person may touch. Each request needs both answers.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Cases: USPS, Peloton and Optus, APIs that trusted too much
md: Adding a login in front of an endpoint is not the fix for broken authorization. Peloton's partial fix and USPS's whole design show the result: every registered user, and anyone can register, gets everyone's data.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM relay: forwarding someone else's login, and how signing stops it
md: Relay borrows a live NTLM sign-in instead of stealing a hash. It is stopped by binding authentication to the session or channel: SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, and EPA on HTTPS. Then remove the bait: LLMNR, NBT-NS and NTLM itself. To respond, isolate the rogue host, review what the relayed identity did on the target, and revoke any certificate issued through a relayed login.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: DCSync: asking a domain controller for every password
md: DCSync abuses a legitimate protocol: anyone with both replication rights can ask a DC for any password hash. Control who holds those rights, audit 4662 with the replication GUIDs, and treat a DCSync as compromise of every account.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Why documents and scripts: the chain an analyst unpicks
md: Every demo in this course uses harmless files built for it. Never fetch real samples onto a work machine: get them only through your organisation's incident process, keep them zipped with a password, and open them only in the isolated lab described in the malware course.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Unpacking II: dumping from memory, and payloads hidden in data
md: Carve, decode, confirm. Find where the code reads data, extract exactly those bytes, decode them step by step, and check each step against the code that does it. A decoding you guessed is a hypothesis until the code agrees.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Return-oriented programming as Shacham defined it
md: Misconception: "ROP needs special gadget functions, so removing dangerous library functions stops it." Shacham's thesis is the opposite: any large enough body of x86 code contains enough sequences, many of them unintended. The fix is checking control flow, not pruning code.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Command and control at the design level
md: Do not treat C2 detection as "find the red team's tool". CISA's federal red team (AA24-193A) "deployed over seven different implants" with different host and network signatures precisely to show that defenders who hunt one framework's fingerprints miss the rest. Detect the behaviour every implant shares: periodic contact, new destinations, odd egress from servers.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Reporting, retesting and where to practise
md: Measure a red or purple team by what it changes: findings with owners, fixes retested with the same procedure, and tests that keep running afterwards. Everything is done under written authorisation, inside agreed rules, with a way to stop in minutes.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: From one model call to an agent loop
md: The model does not execute tools. It only emits a structured request. Whether a shell command actually runs, and with what permissions, is decided entirely by harness code, which is why safety controls belong in the harness.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The read path: scoring memories by recency, importance and relevance
md: Recency decay does not resolve conflicts. A stale fact with high importance and relevance still makes the cut, so the newer fact helps only if the reader happens to trust it more. Resolve contradictions on the write path; use scoring to choose among facts that are all still true.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
md: An agentic RL environment is a benchmark task turned into a loop you can run millions of times: `reset` to a clean sandbox, `step` per tool call, and a programmatic checker that produces the reward at the end. The simulated user in tau-bench is part of the environment, not part of the policy.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
md: The dangerous line is never the model call. It is the loop that turns model output into actions. Put your controls there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Model supply chain: pickle files, safetensors and signing
md: Loading a pickle is running code. Prefer safetensors, load PyTorch files with weights_only=True, and verify a signature or hash from a source you trust before loading anything.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Cheap surrogates for DFT: graph networks and interatomic potentials
md: Judge a discovery surrogate by what it does to DFT spending: precision (hit rate), recall, and DAF on unrelaxed inputs. A low regression error does not guarantee good decisions near the hull.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a green-list watermark and detector in 60 lines
md: The two p-values for the watermarked run differ by a factor of about 78,000 ($5.9 \times 10^{-30}$ versus $4.6 \times 10^{-25}$). Both are tiny here, but the same gap at a borderline score decides whether someone is accused. Three Bricks reports exact tests because the normal tail is too optimistic exactly where thresholds sit, deep in the tail.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
md: What interposition misses: statically linked programs (LD_PRELOAD is a feature of the dynamic linker), secure-execution binaries such as set-user-ID programs (the linker ignores LD_PRELOAD paths with slashes), and any memory that bypasses malloc: direct mmap, custom arenas and pools, GPU allocations. heaptrack's README notes pool allocators need code annotations to be profiled.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: LOF answers a different question from Isolation Forest: not how isolated a point is, but how isolated it is relative to its own neighborhood. Use it when normal data has regions of very different density; pay for it with k-nearest-neighbor searches and a k to tune.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023), item by item
md: Most of the API Top 10 is not exotic. It is a missing check (who owns this, who may call this, how many times), a forgotten endpoint, or misplaced trust in another system.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OpenID Connect: logging users in with an ID token
md: ID token: for the client, proves a login happened (check aud = your client_id and nonce). Access token: for the API, grants access (the API checks aud = itself). Never accept one where the other is expected.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to API and token attacks
md: Tokens move the security perimeter into data: who issued it, with which key, for which audience, for how long. Log those fields on every request, alert on the impossible ones, and rehearse revoking at scale.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Writing rules: Semgrep and CodeQL on the same code
md: Write a custom rule when a bug teaches you a pattern: after every incident or review finding, ask "where else does this pattern appear?" and encode it. That is variant analysis, and it turns one fix into a class fix.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: SSVC: decisions instead of scores
md: SSVC turns "how bad is it?" into "what do we do, and how fast?". The inputs that matter most are exploitation status and your own context: exposure and how essential the system is. A score cannot know the second.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
md: ARIES in one line: **repeat history, then undo the losers, logging every undo as a redo-only CLR whose UndoNextLSN skips what is already undone**. That makes recovery **idempotent**, meaning that running it again after a partial run ends in the same state as running it once: crash during analysis or redo and you simply start over; crash during undo and you resume where the CLRs say.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
md: `gather` does not cancel siblings on failure. With the default `return_exceptions=False`, the first exception propagates to the caller but the docs state the other awaitables "won't be cancelled and will continue to run". If you want per-item errors without losing the batch, pass `return_exceptions=True` and inspect each result; if one failure should stop everything, use a `TaskGroup`.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Cooperative scheduling: blocking, budgets and cancellation
md: The budget only helps tasks that keep awaiting **Tokio** resources. It cannot interrupt a tight CPU loop or a blocking call, and the Tokio team has said it will not detect blocked workers and add threads automatically. Fixing those is your job.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: From a waveform to 0.96 s log-mel patches
md: A pretrained audio model never sees a whole clip at once. It sees fixed 0.96 s log-mel patches and returns one embedding and one score vector per patch. Everything about clip-level decisions (lesson 3) is about combining those per-patch outputs.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: How offline cracking works: guesses, lists, rules and arithmetic
md: Offline cracking = guess, hash, compare, at the attacker's full hardware speed. Defenders control two things: how many guesses a password needs (length, unpredictability, blocklists) and how expensive each guess is (a slow, salted hash).

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Wearing MFA down: SIM swaps, push fatigue and Uber 2022
md: MFA is only as strong as its weakest step. SMS inherits the phone network's weaknesses; plain push inherits human fatigue. Number matching helps against fatigue; phishing-resistant MFA removes the whole class.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: End-to-end science agents: AI Scientist and co-scientist
md: End-to-end science agents fail at the steps where nothing external checks them: invented numbers, unfair comparisons, edits to their own limits. Put independent checks (sandboxes, reproducibility, human experts) at exactly those points.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: x86-64 on Linux and macOS: the System V calling convention
md: Do not apply Windows habits to Linux binaries. On Windows the first argument is in `rcx`; on Linux and macOS `rcx` is the fourth. Misreading the convention shifts every argument by several positions and makes a correct analysis look nonsensical. Check the file format first: PE means Microsoft x64, ELF or Mach-O on x86-64 means System V.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Ternary weights: log2(3), absmean and the power of zero
md: "1-bit LLM" is the family name, not the bit count. BitNet b1.58 weights are ternary (about 1.58 bits), the original BitNet was binary (1 bit), and in both the activations are 8-bit and the embeddings stay in higher precision.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Counters and history: how a predictor learns a pattern
md: Predictors learn *regularity*: biased branches, periodic patterns, and (next lesson) correlations with other branches. A branch on random data with a 50/50 split is mispredicted about half the time on every CPU, no matter how clever the predictor.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
md: Bloom filters only help point lookups. A range scan must open every run that overlaps the range and merge them, so the RocksDB guide counts scan read amplification as (L0 files) + (non-empty levels). Tiered layouts with many runs pay most for scans.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: 2Q, InnoDB midpoint insertion and PostgreSQL ring buffers
md: Real systems combine a cheap recency approximation with a second signal: PostgreSQL uses counts plus per-operation rings, InnoDB uses a two-segment list with a time threshold, and 2Q and LRU-2 use a remembered first reference. The common goal: a page must prove reuse before it can displace the hot set.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: High availability is not disaster recovery: GitLab, January 2017
md: High availability copies every change, good or bad, as fast as it can; it protects against component failure. Disaster recovery needs copies that did *not* follow the bad change: point-in-time backups or snapshots, kept separately. Ask of every copy: which failures does it survive?

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: When the building burns: OVHcloud 2021 and DR site strategies
md: A disaster recovery copy must sit outside the failure domain of the disaster: another building is not enough if the site is isolated, another zone is not enough if the control plane deletes both. Pick a site or cloud strategy by RTO and cost, and fail over with the most available mechanisms.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Common misconception: byte models are slow because attention is quadratic. Efficient attention (methods and kernels such as FlashAttention that make attention cheaper or faster) helps small models, but the BLT authors point out that at scale the cost is dominated by the large feed-forward layers that run on **every** position. Fewer positions through the big network is what matters.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
md: Limitations the authors list: their FLOP matching is theoretical and the implementation may not yet match token models in wall-clock time; the entropy model is trained separately rather than end to end; and they borrowed BPE scaling-law data ratios that may not be optimal for BLT. BPE still won word deletion and word insertion on CUTE.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: unsafe: five extra powers, same borrow checker
md: `unsafe` does not change the rules; it changes who checks them. Rust programs must never cause undefined behavior, inside or outside unsafe blocks. Inside, the proof obligation moves from the compiler to you.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: A common misconception is that memory cost is proportional to the bytes your code reads. It is proportional to the **lines it touches**. Reading 8 bytes from each of 1,000 scattered lines moves 64,000 bytes through the hierarchy.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Transcoders and cross-layer transcoders
md: Collapsing chains is not free. If the real model really runs a mutually reinforcing loop (the paper sees Copenhagen and Denmark features exciting each other with per-layer transcoders), a CLT can hide it. Simpler graphs can mean less faithful graphs.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Lab: trace, label and intervene on a real graph with circuit-tracer
md: Graph, then labels, then interventions, then a report that names its own gaps. The graph proposes; only the measured change in the real model, including the swaps that fail, counts as evidence.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: XSS: when your page runs someone else's code
md: An `HttpOnly` session cookie does not make XSS harmless. It stops script from *reading* the cookie, so the attacker cannot take the session home. But the injected script does not need the cookie value: it sends requests from the victim's own browser, and the browser attaches the cookie for it.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to client-side attacks
md: Prevention lives in code (encode, sanitise, safe sinks, tokens, allowlists). Detection lives mostly in the browser (CSP and Trusted Types reports) and in monitoring of what your pages load. A team that only watches server logs is blind to DOM XSS and skimmers.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Reading CloudTrail like a responder: who really made this call?
md: Misconception: "the event names the role, so the role's owner did it". A role is a costume many identities can put on. Attribution needs the chain: issued key to used key, back to a long-term credential, a federated sign-in or a workload.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Uber 2022: from one contractor's login to the cloud consoles
md: Misconception: "the CloudTrail logs show no data access, so the cloud was not affected". If an attacker held a vault administrator account, every stored credential must be treated as exposed. Absence of use in the logs you have narrows the impact; it does not remove the need to rotate.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Graphing attack paths: role chains, PMapper and Access Analyzer
md: Least privilege is a property of the graph, not of one policy. Ask "who can reach this role or this data, through any chain?", fix the cheapest edge on each path, and rerun the analysis after every IAM change.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: IAM from zero: users, groups, roles and the JSON policy
md: IAM starts from deny. A request is allowed only if some applicable policy explicitly allows it and no applicable policy explicitly denies it. Write policies as a list of what is needed, never as a list of what to forbid.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Catching misconfigurations early: infrastructure as code and CSPM
md: Scanners produce a lot of findings, and most teams drown in them. Rank by what an attacker could do: public exposure of sensitive data, wildcard IAM on roles reachable from the internet, IMDSv1 on internet-facing instances and disabled logging come before "detailed monitoring is off". A posture tool is only as good as the triage behind it.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Choosing k: elbow, silhouette and their limits
md: Five criteria on the same ten points: the elbow is ambiguous, VRC says k = 5, silhouette says k = 3, BIC with a variance floor says k = 3, and the gap statistic says one cluster. That disagreement is the lesson. Schubert's advice is to use a baseline-aware criterion (VRC, BIC or the gap statistic) rather than an elbow, and to spend your effort on preprocessing, "because garbage in, garbage out".

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: From tuple-at-a-time to vector-at-a-time execution
md: Vectorization keeps the iterator model but changes its unit from one tuple to a cache-sized vector. That amortizes interpretation overhead (small n is bad) without materializing whole columns in RAM (huge n is bad).

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Inlining matters less for the call it removes than for what it enables: constant folding, dead code removal and vectorization inside the merged body. It costs code size, and it only works when the callee's body is visible in the same compilation.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: PGO, -march and fast-math can each beat any -O level, but each adds a condition: representative profiles, a known target CPU, and numerics that tolerate reordering.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Safety: sandboxes, confirmations and prompt injection
md: Assume the model will sometimes be wrong or hijacked, and design so that it does not matter much: isolate the machine, keep secrets and broad network access out of it, require a human for irreversible actions, and check every action before it runs.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
md: Use loom to search **schedules** of a tiny test exhaustively, and TSan to check **ordering** on real runs of the whole program. Neither proves correctness alone; together they cover far more than any number of stress runs.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Why quorum overlap alone is not linearizable, and the fix
md: W + R greater than N guarantees that a read sees every *completed* write. Linearizability also needs reads to agree with each other while a write is in flight. ABD gets that by making each read finish only after its result sits on a quorum.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Elasticsearch bool: filter context versus query context
md: A `should` clause is not an OR filter when the query also has a `filter` or `must` clause, because minimum_should_match then defaults to 0. Putting a hard requirement in `should` silently turns it into a mere preference. Set `minimum_should_match` explicitly if you need at least one of several options to match.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: CP-SAT in practice: lazy clauses, models and statuses
md: Common mistakes. **CP-SAT works over integers only**: a coefficient like 0.5 must be scaled (multiply the constraint by 2). A status of `FEASIBLE` after a time limit is not a proof of optimality, and `UNKNOWN` is not a proof of infeasibility. With more than one worker, runs are not guaranteed to be repeatable; tests and demos often set `num_workers = 1`.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime settings that switch the fences off
md: privileged, extra capabilities, hostPath, runtime sockets, hostPID and hostNetwork each turn a container back into a process on the host. If a workload asks for one, ask why, and isolate it if the answer is real.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Pod Security Admission and policy engines
md: Misconception: "we enforce Restricted, so pods are safe". PSA checks pod fields only. It does not check the image, RBAC, network policy or which Secrets are mounted, and namespaces or users can be exempted in its configuration. It is one layer.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime detection with Falco and the Kubernetes audit log
md: Misconception: "we have audit logging, so we would see an attack". The audit log sees API requests. An attacker who never calls the API server (kubelet exec, a runtime escape, a miner in an existing pod) leaves no audit events. Pair it with node-level runtime detection and network flow logs.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Model the state as a fixed schema where every slot is present and null means unconstrained. Each turn applies one of a few explicit operations per slot, and carryover is the default.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
md: Misconception: "if every step of the CoT is correct, the CoT explains the answer." Turpin et al. found unfaithful CoTs with no obvious errors. Checking that reasoning is *valid* tests plausibility. Only a counterfactual (change an input the CoT ignores and see if the answer moves) tests faithfulness.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: CoT monitors, and what training against them does
md: Misconception: "the monitor flags less often after training, so the model behaves better." A falling flag rate is what both genuine improvement and obfuscation look like. Without an independent ground-truth check of the behavior, you cannot tell them apart.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
md: Overlap hides the smaller stages behind the largest one; it never removes the largest one. Your speedup ceiling is $(\sum_s t_s) / (\max_s t_s)$, reached as $n$ grows, and in the steady state the pipeline runs at the rate of its slowest stage. Before adding streams, work out which stage that is. If it is already the kernel, overlap buys you the copies and nothing more.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Serving it: latency for 100 candidates and distillation
md: Reranker latency is about k divided by throughput. You control it with three knobs: how many candidates you rerank, how large the model is, and how many pairs you can run in parallel. Each trades against accuracy or cost.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: MACs and HMAC: integrity with a shared key
md: Never build a MAC from hash(key + message), and never compare secrets with ==. Use HMAC (or an AEAD, which includes a MAC) and hmac.compare_digest.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Bleichenbacher and ROBOT: retiring RSA key exchange
md: "We patched the oracle" is weaker than "we removed RSA key exchange". ROBOT found new oracles in implementations that already had Bleichenbacher countermeasures, because a single timing or TCP behaviour difference is enough.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Downgrade and protocol confusion: one key, one purpose
md: Security is set by the weakest place a key is accepted and the weakest option a negotiation allows. Give each key one job in one protocol, put the job's name inside everything it signs, and remove options rather than defending them.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
md: A Hopper CUTLASS mainloop is a ring of shared memory stages: a producer warp keeps TMA loads ahead, consumer warpgroups run wgmma on full stages, and full and empty barriers pass ownership of each stage back and forth.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Treat CXL memory as a far NUMA node: same instructions, same caching, about 70 to 100 ns more per miss for a nearby device, bandwidth comparable to a DDR channel per x8 link. Whether it is a win depends on how many misses you send there.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Van Buren (2021): gates up or down, not good or bad motives
md: After Van Buren: 'without authorization' asks whether you may enter the system at all; 'exceeds authorized access' asks whether you entered an area your access does not extend to. Motive is not the test. DOJ policy adds: decline good-faith research, and do not charge contract-only theories.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Copyright and trade secrets: DMCA section 1201 and Megamos Crypto
md: The exemption itself says it is "not a safe harbor from, or defense to" other laws, naming the CFAA. Circumventing a TPM on someone else's server can be legal under 1201 and still be unauthorised access. And the exemption covers the act of circumvention, not distributing circumvention tools.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Professional ethics: ISC2, ACM, the Menlo Report and the UMN patches
md: "The IRB said it was not human research" and "no bug was merged" did not end the matter. Ethics review is a floor, like law. If your study manipulates people's behaviour, they are participants, whatever the form says.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: Domain weights are not a zero-sum allocation of quality. Because very easy and very noisy domains need few samples, and domains transfer to each other, a better mixture can lower loss on **every** domain at once, including the ones it shrinks.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
md: Think in two levels. **Within** a domain, clean and filter documents (lesson 9's rules and deduplication, then a classifier). **Across** domains, choose weights with a method like DoReMi or a fitted mixing model. Then rerun the mixing step, because filtering changes each domain's size and difficulty.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Seeing security from the data's side: copies, states and stages
md: Start every data security question from the data: what is it, where are *all* its copies (including tickets, exports and backups), who can read each one, how can it leave, and when will each copy be destroyed.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security I: accounts, grants, views and the revoke trap
md: Separate owner, application, analyst and admin roles; grant explicit columns or views rather than whole tables; never rely on revoking one column from a table-level grant; and keep grants in version control so drift is visible.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: An alarm nobody should trip: why deception detects
md: A decoy has no legitimate users, so the number of things that touch it is tiny. That, not cleverness, is where its signal comes from. Every design choice in this course protects that property.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Deception in Active Directory: honey accounts and honey SPNs
md: Your own tools will touch decoys: vulnerability scanners, identity-governance jobs that read every account, auditors' scripts, and secret scanners that verify the keys they find (TruffleHog's check calls sts:GetCallerIdentity, which fires a decoy AWS key). List them before go-live and route their hits to a review queue, not to silence. A decoy that a weekly script trips is a decoy everyone learns to ignore.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
md: Determinism leaks are easy to write. Reading the real clock, spawning an OS thread, seeding from OS entropy, or iterating a hash map whose order is randomized per process (Rust's default `HashMap` is) all make the same seed produce different runs. FoundationDB avoids multithreaded concurrency entirely and deploys one node per core instead.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Caches and artifacts: how Ultralytics was poisoned
md: Anything a privileged job reads (a cache, an artifact, a downloaded tool, a config file) is part of its input. Ask who could have written it. If the answer includes a fork, a PR or a comment, the privileged job must treat it as untrusted data or not read it at all.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Build it: turn your GPT into a masked diffusion LM
md: The first attempt kept the GPT's learned position table (wpe). The diffusion model stalled: after 5,000 steps its bound was 2.94 nats per character against the GPT's 1.52. Swapping in rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which LLaDA uses, fixed it: with RoPE the bound reached 1.96 after only 3,000 steps.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput is not throughput. A colocated GPU at 4 req/s still produces plenty of tokens per second, but in the toy run only 29% of requests meet both SLOs. If you only tracked throughput, that overloaded point would look like the best one.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: NTFS and the master file table, record by record
md: A free MFT record with a resident `$DATA` still contains the old file's bytes. A large file's record holds only runs, and those clusters may already belong to someone else. Always check whether the clusters a deleted record points to are now allocated before trusting the content.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Trusting your tools: Cellebrite, Signal (2021) and validation
md: A matching hash proves the evidence did not change. It does not prove your tool read it correctly or that your report is untampered. Validation and independent cross-checks cover that gap.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: The DPO loss on one preference pair, with real numbers
md: The weight $\sigma(\hat r_l - \hat r_w)$ is what makes DPO work. The authors report that a naive version without this weighting (push chosen up, rejected down, equally on every pair) can make the language model degenerate.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Turning on dual writes does not make the stores identical. It only covers objects written *after* the switch. Objects that are never updated again stay only in the old store until the backfill copies them.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: eBPF lets you run your own logic at the moment an event happens, inside the kernel, with a load-time proof that it cannot crash or hang the machine. bpftrace makes that a one-liner: probe, optional filter, action, and maps that summarize in the kernel.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Pruning does not automatically make a model smaller or faster. The LiteRT docs state that pruned models are the same size on disk and have the same latency; they only compress better. You get size savings from a sparse format or compression, and speed only from kernels or hardware that skip zeros. With 8-bit values plus 8-bit gaps, sparse storage only wins once more than half the weights are zero.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: PAN-OS GlobalProtect, 2024: a cookie that became a command
md: Early interim guidance can be wrong. The first CVE-2024-3400 advisory tied exposure to telemetry; that was later corrected. Use a vendor workaround to buy hours, then install the fix and verify, rather than treating the workaround as the answer.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
md: Plain SFT on short samples barely helped here (a 2.0% cut on MATH500). Imitating short traces is weaker than contrasting short against long, because the model never sees what it should move away from.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Underthinking and early exit: stopping at the right moment
md: Waste has two shapes: thinking past a settled answer (stop it with a confidence test such as DEER) and abandoning good ideas too fast (slow the switching with TIP). Both are cheap decode-time controls that need no retraining, sitting between the RL methods and an API's blunt output cap.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Many spellings of one value: UTF-8 overlongs and base64 slack
md: An encoding is safe to check only if every value has exactly one valid spelling and every decoder rejects the rest.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Bidirectional text and Trojan Source (CVE-2021-42574)
md: Reviewers approve what they see; compilers build what is stored. Any character that changes one without the other (bidi controls, unusual line separators, lookalike identifiers) should fail the build unless it is written as a visible escape.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: ETW: providers, sessions and consumers
md: ETW is plumbing: providers emit, sessions buffer, consumers read. Most of what Event Viewer, Sysmon and EDR sensors show you rides on it, so an attacker who can switch providers off removes evidence before it is ever written.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Tampering and EDR killers: SUNBURST, BYOVD and AuKill
md: Check your driver-load filter against this case. SwiftOnSecurity's config excludes event 6 for drivers whose signature contains `microsoft`. The driver AuKill abused was signed by Microsoft, so that exclusion would hide its load. Narrow exclusions to drivers you have inventoried, or match against a vulnerable-driver hash list instead of the signer.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
md: Every NILM method injects prior knowledge to resolve an unidentifiable sum. Hart hand-designs it (step signatures), FHMMs encode it as state machines, and neural nets learn it from sub-metered houses. The test that matters is a house the model never saw.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
md: General-purpose embedding models do not know your abbreviations (`SWE` software engineer, `SDET` software development engineer in test, `RN` registered nurse) and blur words that share context (`sales engineer` vs `software engineer`). Expand abbreviations before embedding, match against many alternate titles rather than one label, and keep an *unknown* outcome instead of forcing the nearest code.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Delegated vs application permissions, and who may consent
md: Delegated means the app is capped by the user; application means the app is capped only by the permission. Restrict who may consent to what, and treat every application permission, especially any with write access, as an admin role held by software.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Devices and the Primary Refresh Token: SSO bound to hardware
md: The PRT is the device's master refresh token. Its strength is the TPM-held session key that signs every use; its weak points are devices without TPMs, attacker-registered devices, and the fact that Conditional Access runs when it is used, not when it is issued.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Taking over admins: help desks, MFA resets and rogue federation
md: Help-desk takeovers turn a phone call into admin credentials, and admin credentials into persistence (federated domains, app secrets, devices). Verify callers out of band, keep admin resets in a small privileged role, require phishing-resistant MFA for admins, and alert on any federation change.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Level-triggered versus edge-triggered, and reading until EAGAIN
md: Level-triggered asks "is it ready now?" on every wait. Edge-triggered says "it just became ready" once. With ET you own the state: read or write until `EAGAIN`, or remember that the connection is still ready.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
md: Count every comparison you make on a query set, including metrics, variants and earlier papers' tests, and correct for the family. Holm is never worse than Bonferroni. Better still, decide the one comparison you will test before you look.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: RELRO, the GOT and FORTIFY_SOURCE
md: RELRO protects a table of pointers by making it read-only after start-up; FORTIFY stops some overflows before they write. Both are cheap, both are build flags, and both should be on: `-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now` and `-D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` at `-O2`.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: How big is a line, how to find false sharing, who pads
md: Do not pad on a hunch. Padding costs memory and can push other hot data out of cache, which is why Drepper calls padding every variable unacceptable. Confirm with perf c2c or a before-and-after benchmark that the line is really contended.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph
md: Predicate subgraph traversal is the right search strategy (no distance computations wasted on failing nodes), but on a normal HNSW graph the predicate subgraph is sparse and disconnected. ACORN changes how the graph is built, or how neighbors are looked up, so that the predicate subgraph stays connected for any predicate.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Build it: a DeepSeekMoE layer with bias balancing in your GPT
md: Do not read quality conclusions off a run this small. Character-level Shakespeare with a 3.65M-parameter MoE (0.9M active) trains in under an hour per run on a CPU; differences of a few thousandths in validation loss between configurations are within seed noise. What this lab shows reliably is the mechanism: what the router does without balancing, and how each method changes the expert loads.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
md: FlashInfer = one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged exactly so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Inductive invariants: from bounded checks to every N
md: An invariant is true in reachable states; an inductive invariant is preserved from *any* state that satisfies it. Model checking finds the first; proofs need the second. Use TLC or Apalache to debug a candidate before you try to prove it. Verus loop invariants, later in the course, carry the same three obligations.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
md: Trace validation is testing, not proof: it checks only the runs you logged, and its verdict depends on choosing the right points in the code to log each atomic step. The paper says plainly that it does not provide formal correctness guarantees. Its strength is that it keeps a spec honest at the cost of logging.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Microscaling: one power-of-two scale per 32 values
md: MX formats move fine-grained scaling into hardware: 32 elements share one power-of-two E8M0 scale, applied by the tensor core during the dot product. For 8-bit elements that works well. For 4-bit elements the power-of-two restriction can waste up to a whole binade of FP4's tiny 3.58-binade range.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Scraping and enumeration: Facebook's 530 million phone numbers
md: Any feature that answers "is this identifier on the service, and whose is it" is an enumeration oracle. Cap it, gate it on consent, minimise its answer and watch its traffic.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fake accounts and Sybil attacks
md: You cannot prove two accounts are two people (Douceur). Make each identity cost something scarce, give new accounts limited power until they earn trust, and look for accounts that act as a group.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Chargebacks, disputes and the true cost of a fraudulent order
md: Chargebacks are the fraud label, and they arrive weeks to months late. A fraudulent order costs goods, shipping and fees, several good orders' worth of margin.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Privacy and fairness of risk models
md: Collect what measurably helps, keep it only as long as needed, and keep it out of other uses. Then measure who your false positives are: an acceptable average can hide an unacceptable burden on one group.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: What vulnerability research is, and the rules you work under
md: Vulnerability research is a loop of find, triage, root-cause, report, fix. Its output is a fixed bug and a regression test, not an exploit, and it starts with permission.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Continuous fuzzing at scale: OSS-Fuzz, ClusterFuzz and Heartbleed
md: Continuous fuzzing turns fuzzing from an event into a property of the project: every commit is fuzzed, every crash is triaged, and fixed reproducers keep guarding the code. If your project parses untrusted input, it belongs in OSS-Fuzz or in ClusterFuzzLite (a lightweight version of ClusterFuzz that runs fuzzers in your CI pipeline).

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
md: Report privately with a minimised reproducer, the sanitizer output, a one-sentence root cause and a suggested fix; agree a disclosure date; publish an advisory with versions and credit once users can patch.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: A hard bin boundary is fragile: noise of a few thousandths can push u from 0.249 to 0.251 and the vote goes to the wrong bin. Practical systems search neighboring bins, or, like Astrometry.net, skip fixed bins and do a radius search in continuous code space.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Distance on a sphere, and why degree boxes break
md: Use great-circle distance for the final answer. The sphere itself is a model: the Earth is slightly flattened, and a spherical model gives errors typically up to 0.3%. That is why PostGIS `geography` defaults to `use_spheroid = true`, and Elasticsearch `geo_distance` defaults to `distance_type: arc` (the faster `plane` is documented as inaccurate over long distances and near the poles).

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Batching: why 32 launches lose to one
md: The per-image resize kernel does 0.44 microseconds of memory work and carries 0.9 to 6.7 microseconds of launch overhead. The GPU is idle or draining for most of the wall clock, and no kernel tuning can recover it. The fix is one launch that covers the whole batch.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Expandable segments: growing one segment with virtual memory
md: Fixed segments freeze their size at cudaMalloc time, so shapes that drift leave slivers. Expandable segments separate virtual addresses from physical memory (reserve once, map chunks as needed), so the segment grows contiguously instead.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
md: Bank = word index mod 32. Different words in one bank serialize; the same word broadcasts. For column access to a 2D tile, make the row width odd.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: SOL percentages are not the score you optimize. The triage guide is blunt about it: validate every change against absolute kernel duration, because SOL percentages can drop while the kernel gets faster, for example when you reduce the total work. Duration is the ground truth, not SOL percent.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG moves work from query time to indexing time. It pays many LLM calls up front to turn the corpus into a graph and a set of pre-written community summaries, so that global questions can be answered by reading summaries instead of sampling chunks.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Failure modes to watch in any LLM-built graph: missed entities in large chunks, duplicate nodes from name variants, hallucinated relationships stated with confidence, and summaries that drop the specific quotes users need. Every later stage inherits these errors, and global answers rarely show the raw evidence.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and R1: RLVR with GRPO at scale
md: "The model discovered reasoning on its own" is an overstatement. Liu et al. (2025, the Dr. GRPO paper you will meet in lesson 7) found that DeepSeek-V3-Base already shows aha-moment style self-reflection before any RL, and the R1 authors themselves say the vivid first-person reasoning style reflects engineered heuristics in the cold-start data. RL amplified behaviors already present in the base model.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Why old attacks still matter: five eras, five patterns
md: Each incident in this course is told the same way: what happened, why it worked (which pattern), what it cost, and what changed. The changes are the useful part: they are the controls you will be asked to run and defend.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Code Red, Slammer and Blaster: worms faster than people
md: "We patch monthly" did not save anyone from Slammer: the patch was six months old. What matters is whether the patch is actually installed on every exposed system, and whether services that need not face the internet (SQL Server's port 1434, Windows RPC) are reachable at all.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: NotPetya: a wiper delivered as a software update
md: NotPetya combined three patterns: a trusted supplier's update, a known flaw left open (EternalBlue) and reusable administrator credentials. Patching stopped only one of them. Unique credentials, segmentation and offline backups, including of the identity system, decided who recovered.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
md: Without precise sampling, the "hot" instruction in `perf annotate` is often the one *after* the slow one, such as the instruction that consumes a load's result. Use `:pp` when you care about individual instructions.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
md: Hardware security in one sentence: the hardware runs your program correctly, but not invisibly. Keep secrets out of shared state (constant-time code, isolation, separate secure processors), keep firmware and microcode current, measure what booted, and expect new variants.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: CL.0 and client-side desync: when a server ignores the body
md: Every code path must leave the connection in a known state: either it consumed exactly the declared body, or it closes the connection. Cache hits, redirects, errors and static files are the paths that forget.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: Huge pages pay off three ways: one TLB entry covers 512 (or 262,144) times more memory, each miss walks fewer levels, and the page tables shrink. The kernel's THP doc calls the fourth effect, one page fault per 2 MiB instead of 512, almost irrelevant because it only happens on first touch.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: Pure SSMs are not simply worse. In the same NVIDIA study, Mamba-2 trained on 3.5T tokens beat the matching Transformer on average across standard zero-shot tasks. The gap is specific: copying, in-context learning and exact retrieval from the prompt.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
md: RRF is not parameter-free. Bruch, Gai and Ingber (TOIS 2023, ACM Transactions on Information Systems) gave each retriever its own k and showed that nDCG swings noticeably when those constants are changed, and that constants tuned in-domain did not transfer reliably out of domain. Also, the window size is a hidden parameter: a document at rank 11 with a window of 10 contributes nothing at all.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
md: Changing a setpoint and changing the program are different. Setpoints are data the program reads (often over the network, by design, from the HMI). The program is the logic itself. Both can steer the process; defenders must watch and protect both.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Case: Ukraine 2015 and Industroyer 2016
md: It is tempting to read 2015 as 'malware turned off the lights'. Investigators found BlackEnergy but could not show it played a role in the outage; people turned off the lights, through legitimate remote access. Monitoring that only looks for malware would have missed it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
md: Misconception: SSO means one session. It means one *login*. After it, the IdP has a session and every app has its own, with its own cookie and lifetime. Disabling a user at the IdP does not end the app sessions already issued (lesson 10).

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Sessions across apps: IdP session, app sessions and logout
md: Offboarding gap: disabling a user at the IdP stops new logins, not existing app sessions or refresh tokens. A complete offboarding or account-takeover response also ends sessions in each app: through back-channel logout or signals where supported, through the app's admin API or SCIM deactivation (next lesson) where not.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
md: A common misconception is that identity and access management means single sign-on. Single sign-on proves who is logging in, once. It says nothing about whether Ana should still hold payroll access three jobs later. Governance works on the access itself, over time.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Just-in-time admin and break-glass accounts
md: A break-glass account that nobody monitors is just a permanent, policy-exempt Global Administrator. Its safety comes entirely from being rare, strongly authenticated, loudly alerted and regularly tested.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
md: Opening deletes every structure that cannot contain the kernel. A real change that is 1 or 2 pixels wide (a crack, a wire, a thin new road at low resolution) is erased along with the noise. Size the kernel from the smallest change you need to keep.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence first: the order of volatility (RFC 3227)
md: RFC 3227 names programs to avoid on a live suspect system, such as `tar` or `xcopy`, because they update the access time of every file they touch, overwriting evidence of what the attacker read.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
md: Clocks start at awareness or determination, not at the end of the investigation. If you wait until you know everything, you will be late. Plan for phased notices: first what you know, then updates.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims
md: Patching closes the door but does not evict anyone already inside. After an injection that may have been exploited, look for persistence (web shells, new accounts, changed configuration) and for what data left, using web, database and network logs.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
md: io_uring turns I/O into **messages in shared memory**: batch them to amortize system calls, register files and buffers to cut per-request work, and use polling modes only where a spare CPU is worth the latency. The price is that correctness (lifetimes, ordering, CQ space) moves into your code.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Signed updates and anti-rollback: what a device must check
md: Fuses are a scarce, permanent budget. Bump the rollback version only when an old image has a security bug worth blocking, as MCUboot's separate security counter allows. Burn the bit only after the new image has proved it works (lesson 10), or a bad update could leave the device unable to boot anything.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Gadgets: from a polluted prototype to code execution (Kibana)
md: Do not read the hardening as "pollution is solved". It closes gadgets inside Node.js's own child_process code only. Your framework, template engine, HTTP client and your own options objects are full of optional properties, and every one is a possible gadget. The fix is still to stop pollution at the source.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution
md: In Electron, every XSS is a candidate for code execution on the user's machine. The defaults (nodeIntegration off, contextIsolation on, sandbox on) are what keep XSS confined to the page; an app that turns any of them off, or runs an old Electron, has removed a wall. Lesson 16 covers the remaining walls you build yourself.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
md: Misconception: "a timeout means the request failed." A timeout means *you stopped waiting*. Writes, compare-and-sets and transaction commits that time out must be recorded as `:info` unless the error proves nothing was applied (for example, the request was rejected before it was sent).

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: The most common autotuning self-deception is a "win" smaller than the confidence interval of the comparison. Report the interval, not just the ratio, and treat an interval that straddles 1.0 as "no difference found", not as a win.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Bypass trades generality for cycles. It wins when per-operation overhead is the bottleneck and you can dedicate cores and devices; it loses when you need the kernel's protocols, tools, filesystems, isolation or power savings.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Temperature: amplifying the small probabilities
md: Temperature does not change the argmax, the class with the highest score. Running the deployed student at T greater than 1 does not change its top-1 predictions at all; it only makes its probabilities less confident. Temperature is a training-time device for distillation (and a separate sampling knob for generative models).

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute
md: Before writing an LLM distillation loss: confirm a teacher exists or will be reused; use logits when you can, text (Seq-KD, traces) when you cannot; store top-k with a tail bucket or mix in data loss; switch to a sorted-probability loss across tokenizers; and consider starting the student from a pruned teacher.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Bits per number are not the whole cost. Group metadata adds bits (about 1 per number for FP16 scale and zero per 32), and the full-precision residual matters for short sequences.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Each tier down is roughly 10x bigger and slower. Offloading turns a prefix-cache miss into a load from a lower tier, which pays off only if the load is faster than recomputing.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: A smaller wall-clock reading does not mean an event happened before another, and an event that did happen first can carry a larger wall-clock reading, as the last-write-wins example shows. Treat wall time as a hint, never as proof of order.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
md: Compression is lossy per vector, and the 1-bit setting does cost measurable quality. Treat 2-bit as the safe default and verify 1-bit on your own evaluation set before shipping it.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
md: The objective never asks a thought to compress the step it replaced. Thoughts are trained only by how much they help predict the remaining steps and the answer, so they are free to become something other than a paraphrase of the text.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: After Coconut: self-distillation, soft thinking, compressed latents
md: Later latent methods differ in what fills the next input slot: a distilled hidden state (CODI), a mixture of token embeddings (Soft Thinking), a sampled compressed embedding (CoLaR) or a discrete code (Token Assorted). Each fixes one of Coconut's limits, and none restores a fully readable trace.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
md: Bigtable's lesson: if you control the layout, make the data follow the model instead of making the model follow the data. Then the prediction is never wrong and there is no last-mile search across blocks.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaRank: weight each pair by what a swap does to NDCG
md: A lambda is a RankNet pair gradient scaled by how much the metric would change if the pair swapped. Pairs that cannot change the top of the list get almost no weight.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Gated DeltaNet: targeted writes plus fast forgetting
md: Gated DeltaNet's one-line change: decay first with a data-dependent $\alpha_t$, then do a delta-rule write with $\beta_t$. $\alpha_t\to0$ clears memory at a context switch; $\alpha_t\to1$ keeps it and lets the delta rule edit single associations.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
md: Owner, then group, then others: the first class that matches is the only one checked. Write octal as 4 for read, 2 for write, 1 for execute, and remember that umask removes bits from every new file.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
md: The journal is stored on disk only if `/var/log/journal` exists or journald is configured with `Storage=persistent`. Otherwise it lives in memory under `/run/log/journal` and is lost at reboot (`journald.conf(5)`). Check this before you need the logs, not after an incident.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tailoring, exceptions and rolling a baseline out safely
md: Tailor per host class, waive per host with an owner and an end date, and store both as code so an expired waiver fails on its own. Roll changes out in rings with a scan between rings.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: eBPF: small verified programs that watch the kernel from inside
md: eBPF lets a verified program run at a kernel hook and filter events in the kernel. That makes it the basis of modern Linux sensors. The verifier checks safety, not intent, so treat every BPF program load as a security event.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: Kinsing and TeamTNT, cryptominers on exposed Linux hosts
md: Cryptojacking chains are short and noisy: an exposed service, a root exploit, a service file, a hiding trick, a miner. A hardened, patched baseline breaks the first two steps, and the audit and eBPF rules from this course flag the rest.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Measuring judge agreement: confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa
md: Always say which agreement number you report. UMBRELA's GPT-4o labels on TREC DL 2019 to 2023 had 4-grade kappa 0.31 to 0.37 but binarised kappa 0.42 to 0.50 on the same labels. A paper quoting one and a dashboard quoting the other are not comparable.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Designing human evaluations and measuring agreement
md: Do not report raw percent agreement alone. With skewed labels (say 90% of pairs are ties) two annotators agree often by chance. Report kappa with the confusion matrix, and say how ties were handled.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
md: Model weights are paid once; KV is paid per token per sequence. A common mistake is to size a deployment by "the model fits on the GPU". A model that fits with 2 GB to spare can serve almost nobody: 2 GB is only about 15,000 tokens of Llama 3 8B's KV cache.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
md: Examples fix the *format*; reasoning before the answer improves the *content* on multi-step problems. Both work only through the context the model reads before it commits to a token.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Ambiguity, negation and graceful fallback
md: Never silently drop a filter the user asked for. A validator that deletes an unknown value and runs the rest turns *rust engineers in Gotham* into *rust engineers anywhere*, and the user believes the results are in Gotham.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
md: FIRST needs two things a plain chat API may not give you: logits over the identifier tokens at the first position, and a model whose first-token logits are trained or validated to rank well. With a zero-shot model, check that the logit order matches its generated order before trusting it.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Why sending every prompt to the strongest model wastes money
md: Routing pays off when two things are true at once: the price gap between models is large, and a sizable share of your prompts are ones where the weak model is just as good. If every prompt is hard, no router can save money without losing quality.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
md: The ratio test needs at least two neighbors, so use `knnMatch(..., k=2)`. A matcher created with `crossCheck=True` is meant for `match()`, which returns one best match per descriptor.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
md: Helping is the general trick for multi-step lock-free updates: leave the structure in a state that any thread can recognise as half-finished and complete on the owner's behalf. Then no thread ever needs to wait for a specific other thread.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
md: T3's baseline is all zeros, so its MAD is 0 and the modified z-score divides by zero. Never let a never-fired template be scored this way: handle it with a separate **first-seen** rule that alerts the first time a template id appears, or when a template's lifetime count crosses a small bound. A miner that reports a new template id gives you that signal for free.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: The detection lifecycle: hypothesis to retirement
md: An alert without a written response is a notification nobody owns. If you cannot say what the analyst should do in the first ten minutes, the detection is not finished.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
md: Each RoPE pair has a wavelength $\lambda_d = 2\pi b^{2d/|D|}$. Pairs with $\lambda_d \ll L$ are safe at any length; pairs with $\lambda_d > L$ are the ones that break when you go past the trained window.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Does the model use its context? Evaluation
md: Do not trust a single number. Low perplexity, a passing passkey test and a large advertised window can all coexist with poor use of mid-context information. Test retrieval at many depths, multi-hop and aggregation tasks, and short-context regressions.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Training for any loop count: random depth and truncated backprop
md: Random iteration counts teach one set of weights to work at many depths. Truncated backprop through only the last $k$ iterations keeps training memory independent of $r$, while the input injection still sends gradient to the prelude.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: LoRA: a frozen weight plus a trainable low-rank update
md: LoRA does not compress or approximate the pretrained weight. W0 keeps all its information at full rank. Only the *change* learned during fine-tuning is restricted to rank r.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO
md: "Loss on the forget set went up" (or its perplexity, $e$ to the average per-token loss, as in the prerequisite course) is not evidence of good unlearning. GA can drive that loss arbitrarily high by wrecking the model. Always read forget metrics next to utility metrics and next to the retrained reference.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Lab: unlearn TOFU authors with NPO, measure it, then quantize it
md: Our run is one seed of a 124M model on 20 authors, with a simplified utility and our own simulated quantizer. Use it to learn the workflow and the failure modes, not as evidence about which method is better at scale; for that, run the framework and report its full metrics.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Persistence on macOS: launchd, login items and BTM
md: Look beyond launchd: Microsoft's Shrootless research showed `~/.zshenv` runs for every zsh, including under `sudo`. Shell startup files, login items and browser extensions are all persistence. A new agent is cheap for the attacker; your job is to make it loud.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: What malware is, and the families analysts name
md: Do not trust the malware's own story. A ransom note, a file name or an icon is chosen by the author. Classify by what the code actually does: NotPetya's note said ransomware, its code said wiper.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: sandboxes, monitors and the WannaCry kill switch
md: Never register or contact infrastructure from a live sample without authorisation and coordination. Hutchins' registration worked out, but researchers who touch attacker infrastructure can disrupt investigations or alert attackers. In your lab, the internet is fake by design.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Why vector size is a cost knob, and why chopping a vector fails
md: Matryoshka training puts the most useful information in the first coordinates, so a prefix of the vector is a good small embedding. Without it, keeping the first m numbers of a normal embedding throws away information almost at random.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
md: Bubble = (p - 1) / (v m). 1F1B bounds activation memory to p microbatches; interleaving divides the bubble by v at the cost of v times more pipeline sends.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Measuring the result: MFU, HFU and what the numbers count
md: Do not compare a paper's achieved TFLOP/s across systems without checking what it counts. Narayanan et al.'s 52% includes recomputation FLOPs; PaLM introduced MFU precisely because HFU depends on implementation choices like rematerialization (another name for recomputation).

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Know normal: the process tree, command lines and the PEB
md: Kernel-side data (EPROCESS, and the VADs of the next lesson) is what the process cannot easily edit; user-side data (PEB, loader lists, command line) is what it can. When they disagree, believe the kernel side and ask why the user side was changed.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Fragmentation is not a leak. In a leak, *live* data grows because the program forgets to free. With fragmentation, live data is flat while the *footprint* grows. Tell them apart by comparing the bytes the allocator says are allocated with the memory it holds: a leak raises both, fragmentation widens the gap.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
md: Myth: "Relaxed writes may take ages to show up, and SeqCst makes them visible sooner." The memory model says nothing about timing at all, only about order. A stronger ordering does not make data travel faster; it may even slow your program down.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: Holding a guard is holding back everyone's garbage. Pinning across a blocking call, a lock wait or a long iteration stops the epoch from advancing for all threads. crossbeam provides `Guard::repin` to briefly unpin and pin again inside long loops; references loaded before the repin are no longer protected.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Where things live: code, static data, heap and stack
md: The bug class tells you how memory is misused; the region tells you what gets damaged. Stack overflows threaten return addresses, heap overflows threaten neighbouring objects and allocator data.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
md: A subtle limit of contrastive loss: it pulls every same-identity pair toward distance 0, so it tries to squash all images of one person onto a single point. The authors of FaceNet (Google's 2015 face recognition system, next lesson) argued that a triplet loss is better suited, because it only asks same-identity images to be closer than other identities, letting one person's images spread out along a region.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time
md: Misconception: "returning or summing the result is enough". Using the output defeats dead-code elimination, but not constant folding. The input must also come from somewhere the compiler cannot see through. JMH's constant-folding sample says to read inputs from non-final fields of a state object, and warns against making them `final` even when your IDE suggests it.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
